config.description: Columnar chart for 65 ÷ 5: dividend digits 6|5 in tens and units columns; remainder 1 from the tens division prefixes the brought-down 5 to make gross dividend 15; quotient digits 1|3 give 13.
config.textual_equivalent: 65 ÷ 5: 6 ÷ 5 = 1 remainder 1; bring down 5 to form gross dividend 15; 15 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 0; quotient digits 1 and 3 give 13.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 65 by 5 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Write the divisor 5 down first. Because 5 has only one digit there is nothing to raise as a flag, so the whole of 5 acts as the main divisor and no crosswise correction will be needed later.
Take the leading dividend digit 6, sitting in the tens column, and divide it by the main divisor 5. It goes in once, so the first quotient digit is 1 and 1 is left over.
Carry that remainder 1 into the next column and bring the units digit 5 down beside it. Read together they form the gross dividend 15 for the units column.
Divide the gross dividend 15 by the main divisor 5. This gives the units quotient digit 3 and leaves remainder 0, so the division closes exactly here.
Read the quotient digits off the columns in order, tens digit 1 then units digit 3. So 65 divided by 5 is 13 with remainder 0.

common_mistakes: Dropping the remainder 1 from the tens column and dividing the bare 5 by 5, which turns the answer into 11 instead of 13.
Hunting for a flag digit inside the one-digit divisor 5 and subtracting a correction this problem does not need.

config.description: Divisor 14 split into main 1 | flag 4 lanes over dividend digits 9|8; a diagonal arrow carries the crosswise product 9×4=36 into the adjustment lane subtracted from 98, leading to the corrected quotient 7.
config.textual_equivalent: 98 ÷ 14, main 1 flag 4: tentative 9 ÷ 1 = 9; crosswise product 9×4 = 36; 98 − 36 = 62; corrected quotient 7 since 7×14 = 98.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 98 by 14 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Write the two-digit divisor 14 with its last digit raised as a flag: the main divisor is 1 and the flag digit is 4. Every trial division from here uses only the 1, and the 4 is charged back afterwards.

solution.operation: Divide first digit by main divisor
solution.description: Divide the leading dividend digit 9 by the main divisor 1, which gives 9. This is only a tentative quotient because the flag digit 4 has not been paid for yet.
Multiply the tentative quotient 9 by the flag digit 4 to get 36. That is the amount the flag has already claimed, and it must come back out of the dividend.

Rebuild the gross dividend from the digits 9 and 8 as 9 tens plus 8, that is 98, then subtract the flag adjustment 36 to leave 62. Since 62 is still far larger than 14, the tentative quotient 9 cannot stand.
Bring the trial quotient down until the flag is paid for exactly. Nine overshoots; testing 7 gives 7 times 14 equals 98, matching the dividend with nothing left over, so the quotient is 7.

common_mistakes: Stopping at the tentative quotient 9 and reporting 98 divided by 14 as 9, without ever subtracting the flag product.
Dividing the first digit 9 by the whole divisor 14 instead of by the main divisor 1 at the trial step.

config.description: Divisor 12 split into main 1 | flag 2 lanes over dividend digits 9|6; the crosswise product 9×2=18 flows diagonally into the adjustment lane (96−18=78) before the quotient is corrected to 8.
config.textual_equivalent: 96 ÷ 12, main 1 flag 2: tentative 9 ÷ 1 = 9; crosswise product 9×2 = 18; 96 − 18 = 78; corrected quotient 8 since 8×12 = 96.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 96 by 12 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Raise the last digit of the divisor 12 as a flag: main divisor 1, flag digit 2. Trial division will use the 1, and the 2 gets charged back through the crosswise product.

solution.operation: Divide first digit by main divisor
solution.description: Divide the leading digit 9 by the main divisor 1, giving the tentative quotient 9. It stays provisional until the flag digit has been accounted for.
Multiply the tentative quotient 9 by the flag digit 2 to get the flag adjustment 18.
Form the gross dividend as 9 tens plus 6, that is 96, and subtract the flag adjustment 18, leaving 78. A leftover of 78 is far bigger than 12, so 9 clearly overshoots.

Reduce the trial quotient and test candidates against the dividend. The estimate 78 divided by 12 is 6.5, which confirms 9 was much too large; working back up, 8 times 12 is exactly 96, so the quotient is 8.

common_mistakes: Treating the estimate 6.5 as the answer and rounding it to 6, when 6 times 12 is only 72.
Forgetting the flag adjustment 18 altogether and keeping the tentative quotient 9.

config.description: Divisor 16 split into main 1 | flag 6 lanes over dividend digits 1|4|4; the crosswise product 14×6=84 feeds the adjustment lane (144−84=60), and the quotient is corrected to 9.
config.textual_equivalent: 144 ÷ 16, main 1 flag 6: tentative 14 ÷ 1 = 14; crosswise product 14×6 = 84; 144 − 84 = 60; corrected quotient 9 since 9×16 = 144.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 144 by 16 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Flag the divisor 16 as main part 1 and flag digit 6, so the trial divisions are done by 1 and the 6 is corrected for afterwards.

solution.operation: Divide first digit by main divisor
solution.description: The leading digit 1 is smaller than the divisor, so take the first two digits 14 together and divide them by the main divisor 1, giving the tentative quotient 14.
Multiply the tentative quotient 14 by the flag digit 6 to get the flag adjustment 84, the share the flag digit has already claimed.
Subtract the flag adjustment 84 from the gross dividend 144, leaving 60. Sixty is still several times 16, so the tentative quotient 14 is much too large.
Pull the quotient down and check it by multiplying back. The estimate 60 divided by 16 is about 3.75, showing how badly 14 overshot; 9 times 16 is exactly 144, so the quotient is 9.

common_mistakes: Dividing only the leading digit 1 by the main divisor instead of taking the first two digits 14 together.
Reporting the tentative quotient 14 as the answer, even though 14 times 16 is 224, far past 144.

config.description: Divisor 13 split into main 1 | flag 3 lanes over dividend digits 1|6|9; the crosswise product 16×3=48 feeds the adjustment lane (169−48=121) with iterated correction converging on quotient 13.
config.textual_equivalent: 169 ÷ 13, main 1 flag 3: tentative 16 ÷ 1 = 16; crosswise product 16×3 = 48; 169 − 48 = 121; iterate the adjustment to reach quotient 13 since 13×13 = 169.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 169 by 13 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Split the divisor 13 into main part 1 and flag digit 3, so every trial division is by 1 and the 3 is settled by subtraction.

solution.operation: Divide first digit by main divisor
solution.description: The single leading digit 1 is too small to divide, so take the first two digits 16 and divide by the main divisor 1, giving the tentative quotient 16.
Multiply the tentative quotient 16 by the flag digit 3 to get the flag adjustment 48.
Subtract the flag adjustment 48 from 169, which leaves 121. That leftover is still far above 13, so 16 remains too large and the estimate has to be lowered and the adjustment redone.
Lower the trial quotient and confirm by multiplying back: 13 times 13 is 169 exactly, with nothing left over, so the quotient is 13.

common_mistakes: Assuming a single flag subtraction always finishes the job and reporting 121 as the remainder.
Using the tentative quotient 16 as the answer, when 16 times 13 is 208 and overshoots 169.

config.description: Divisor 12 split into main 1 | flag 2 lanes over dividend digits 8|4; the crosswise product 8×2=16 feeds the adjustment lane (84−16=68) before the quotient is corrected to 7.
config.textual_equivalent: 84 ÷ 12, main 1 flag 2: tentative 8 ÷ 1 = 8; crosswise product 8×2 = 16; 84 − 16 = 68; corrected quotient 7 since 7×12 = 84.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 84 by 12 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Write 12 as main divisor 1 with the digit 2 raised as a flag, so the trial division uses the 1 alone.
Divide the leading digit 8 by the main divisor 1 to get the tentative quotient 8, which still has to be corrected for the flag digit.
Multiply the tentative quotient 8 by the flag digit 2 to get the flag adjustment 16.
Subtract the flag adjustment 16 from the gross dividend 84, leaving 68. That is still well above 12, which shows the tentative quotient 8 is too large.
Bring the trial quotient down and verify against the dividend. The estimate 68 divided by 12 is about 5.67, and testing candidates near it, 7 times 12 is exactly 84, so the quotient is 7.

common_mistakes: Rounding the estimate 5.67 to 6 and stopping, when 6 times 12 is only 72 and leaves 12 unaccounted for.
Multiplying the flag digit 2 by the units digit 4 instead of by the tentative quotient 8.

config.description: Divisor 13 split into main 1 | flag 3 lanes over dividend digits 1|5|6; the crosswise product 15×3=45 feeds the adjustment lane (156−45=111) with iteration converging on quotient 12.
config.textual_equivalent: 156 ÷ 13, main 1 flag 3: tentative 15 ÷ 1 = 15; crosswise product 15×3 = 45; 156 − 45 = 111; iterate the adjustment to reach quotient 12 since 13×12 = 156.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 156 by 13 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Split the divisor 13 into main part 1 and flag digit 3, and set the dividend digits 1, 5 and 6 under those lanes.
The leading 1 is smaller than the divisor, so divide the first two digits 15 by the main divisor 1, giving the tentative quotient 15.
Multiply the tentative quotient 15 by the flag digit 3 to get the flag adjustment 45.
Subtract the adjustment 45 from 156, leaving 111. Since 111 is still many times 13, one pass is not enough and the trial quotient has to be reduced again.
Settle the quotient by multiplying back: 13 times 12 is 156 exactly, so the quotient is 12 with no remainder.

common_mistakes: Keeping the tentative quotient 15, even though 15 times 13 is 195 and overshoots 156.
Reading the 111 left after the first adjustment as the remainder instead of as a signal to lower the quotient.

config.description: Divisor 15 split into main 1 | flag 5 lanes over dividend digits 1|8|0; the crosswise product 18×5=90 feeds the adjustment lane (180−90=90), verified as quotient 12.
config.textual_equivalent: 180 ÷ 15, main 1 flag 5: tentative 18 ÷ 1 = 18; crosswise product 18×5 = 90; 180 − 90 = 90; quotient 12 since 15×12 = 180.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 180 by 15 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Raise the last digit of 15 as a flag: main divisor 1, flag digit 5, with the dividend digits 1, 8 and 0 lined up beside them.
Because the leading 1 is smaller than the divisor, divide the first two digits 18 by the main divisor 1, which gives the tentative quotient 18.
Multiply the tentative quotient 18 by the flag digit 5, giving the flag adjustment 90 to be taken back out of the dividend.

Subtract the adjustment 90 from 180, leaving 90. A leftover that large shows 18 was far too big, so lower the trial quotient and check by multiplying back: 15 times 12 is exactly 180, fixing the quotient at 12.

common_mistakes: Taking the tentative quotient 18 as the answer instead of correcting for the flag digit 5.
Seeing 180 minus 90 leave 90 and reporting 90 as the remainder rather than reducing the quotient.

config.description: Divisor 14 split into main 1 | flag 4 lanes over dividend digits 1|9|6; the crosswise product 19×4=76 feeds the adjustment lane (196−76=120) with iterated correction to quotient 14.
config.textual_equivalent: 196 ÷ 14, main 1 flag 4: tentative 19 ÷ 1 = 19; crosswise product 19×4 = 76; 196 − 76 = 120; iterate the adjustment to reach quotient 14 since 14×14 = 196.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 196 by 14 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Split the divisor 14 into main part 1 and flag digit 4, placing the dividend digits 1, 9 and 6 under the lanes.
The leading 1 will not carry a division on its own, so divide the first two digits 19 by the main divisor 1 for a tentative quotient of 19.
Multiply the tentative quotient 19 by the flag digit 4 to get the flag adjustment 76.
Subtract the adjustment 76 from the dividend 196, leaving 120. That leftover is still far larger than 14, so one correction is not enough and the trial quotient must come down again.
Fix the quotient by multiplying back: 14 times 14 is 196 exactly, so 196 divided by 14 is 14 with no remainder.

common_mistakes: Stopping at the tentative quotient 19, which multiplied by 14 gives 266, far beyond 196.
Treating the 120 left after the first adjustment as the final remainder.

config.description: Columnar chart for 504 ÷ 24 (main 2, flag 4): 5÷2 writes 2 remainder 1; the remainder prefixes the brought-down 0 to make 10; the flag product 2×4=8 is subtracted in that column to leave 2; columns build quotient 21.
config.textual_equivalent: 504 ÷ 24 with main 2 and flag 4: 5 ÷ 2 = 2 remainder 1; bring down 0 to form 10; subtract flag product 8 to leave 2; continue to quotient 21.

examples.problem_statement: Divide 504 by 24 using the Dhvajanka Sutra (Flag Division method).

solution.description: Write the divisor 24 with its last digit raised: main divisor 2 and flag digit 4. Unlike the divisors beginning with 1, the main divisor here is 2, so the column divisions are real divisions by 2.
Divide the leading dividend digit 5, in the hundreds column, by the main divisor 2. It goes in twice with 1 left over, so the first quotient digit is 2 and the remainder 1 passes to the next column.
Multiply the quotient digit 2 just written by the flag digit 4, giving 8. That is the flag's claim on the next column and must be subtracted there.
Carry the remainder 1 into the tens column and bring down the digit 0 beside it to make 10, then subtract the flag adjustment 8, leaving a net 2 to divide in that column.
Carry the same routine through the remaining column and check the result: the quotient digits read 21, and 21 times 24 is 504, confirming the answer.

common_mistakes: Dividing the leading 5 by the whole divisor 24 instead of by the main divisor 2, which stalls the first column at 0.
Bringing the 0 down to make 10 but forgetting to subtract the flag product 8 before dividing that column.
